title: How Finland Held Off Stalin's Army for 105 Days
summary:
In November 1939, the Soviet Union, with about 170 million people, attacked Finland, a country of under four million. Moscow had asked for a border moved away from Leningrad and a naval base at Hanko, and Finland had said no. The Red Army crossed the border on November 30 and expected little trouble.

This map-based explainer follows the Winter War step by step: the secret Soviet-German deal, the shelling of Mainila, the Mannerheim Line, the forest ambushes at Suomussalmi and the Raate Road, the sniper called the White Death, the Soviet breakthrough in February, and the peace that cost Finland land but not its independence. #WinterWar #History #Maps

caveats: Casualty figures are estimates. Finland's 25,904 dead or missing is the commonly cited Finnish figure; Soviet figures of about 127,000 to 168,000 dead or missing are low-end modern estimates and are disputed. Soviet-era and later claims range higher, including Khrushchev's figure of one million total losses, which is almost certainly inflated.

Force sizes and tank counts differ by source: 2,514 to 6,541 Soviet tanks, and 425,000 to 760,000 Soviet soldiers at the start in some counts, with over a million near the border in others. Finland had at most about 300,000 under arms.

The quote about the Finnish soldier standing in the snow is attributed to Mannerheim in secondary sources; it is paraphrased here. Simo Hayha's 500+ kill count is a credited figure and cannot be fully verified.
The 300,000 shells in a day is one estimate for a Soviet artillery sector in February 1940 and may not apply to the whole front.

Maps are simplified and redrawn for this video; borders, front lines and town locations are approximate (roughly 15 to 30 miles), and the ceded territory changes color in large blocks rather than along the exact line.

shorts.hook: How did Finland trap two divisions?
shorts.title: The Firewood Trap That Stopped an Army

shorts.hook: Why is it called a Molotov cocktail?
shorts.title: The Joke Behind the Molotov Cocktail

beats.say: In 1939, the Soviet Union, a country of about 170 million people, attacked Finland, a country with under four million. Finland fought back for 105 days, and it stayed independent. So who actually won?
That's the Winter War. It ran from November 30, 1939, to March 13, 1940, and it ended with Finland still free, but a lot smaller.
To see how that happened, start with a number. In 1939, the city of Leningrad sat only about 20 miles from the Finnish border.
In August 1939, Germany and the Soviet Union signed a pact. A secret part of it put Finland in the Soviet sphere of influence. Finland wasn't in the room.
That October, Stalin and Molotov met Finland's negotiator in Moscow. They wanted the border on the Karelian Isthmus moved back from Leningrad, some islands, and a rented naval base at Hanko.
In return, Moscow offered a bigger piece of Soviet Karelia. About twice the size of the land it wanted. Sounds fair, right?
The catch was where the land was. Finland's best defenses sat right on the Isthmus, inside the zone Moscow wanted. Giving it up meant giving up the fortifications too.
Finland offered the islands and a smaller shift of the border. It said no to the naval base. In mid-November, the Finnish team went home with no deal.
Finland used the stalling time. It called up its army, and it asked Sweden, Britain, and France for help. Very little came of that, and the Finns knew they might face this alone.
On November 26, Moscow said Finnish guns had shelled a Soviet village called Mainila. Seven shots, it said, and four soldiers killed.

Finland said its guns were too far back to reach that spot. Most historians now think the Soviets shelled their own side as an excuse. In the next few days, Moscow cancelled its non-aggression pact and cut off relations.
At 8 AM on November 30, the Red Army crossed the border. There was no declaration of war. Bombers hit Helsinki the same day.

The next day, Moscow announced a new government of Finland, set up in Terijoki, the first town its troops took. It was led by a Finnish communist named Otto Kuusinen. Finns rallied around their real government instead.
The League of Nations kicked the Soviet Union out on December 14. It was a strong message. It didn't stop a single tank.
Look at the numbers. The Red Army had more than a million soldiers near the border. At its peak, Finland had about 300,000.
In the air, it was about 2,300 Soviet planes against 114 Finnish ones. Finland had around 32 tanks. Moscow had thousands, though the exact count is disputed.
Finland's big defense was the Mannerheim Line, across the Karelian Isthmus. It wasn't one giant wall. It was trenches, barbed wire, and 221 bunker systems tucked between lakes and swamps.
The line's namesake, Marshal Mannerheim, is said to have called the real defense the Finnish soldier standing in the snow. That turned out to be the whole plan.
The Red Army came in along eight main routes, across a border about 800 miles long. The biggest push went straight at the Isthmus, aimed at Viipuri.
In the south, Soviet tanks ran into the Mannerheim Line and stalled. Finnish troops stopped them with mines, anti-tank guns, and bottles of burning gasoline.
Far to the north, near the Arctic coast, the Soviets also pushed at Salla and Petsamo. Finland had to defend every one of those fronts, with far fewer men than the Red Army had.
It was freezing. Temperatures fell as low as 45 degrees below zero Fahrenheit. The Finns had winter gear and skis. Many Soviet soldiers had little winter training and no skis.

Finland also moved supplies the old-fashioned way. Horses and reindeer hauled food and ammunition through the forest. One reindeer could pull a sleigh with about 660 pounds of supplies for eight hours.
On December 12, at Tolvajärvi, the Finns beat a Soviet force and pushed it back. It was the first big Finnish win, and it showed the Red Army could be beaten.
Up north, the Soviet 163rd Division pushed toward the village of Suomussalmi. The plan was to cut Finland in half at its narrowest point, and reach the city of Oulu.
A second division, the 44th, came down a narrow forest road from the border to help. That road was the only way in, and the only way out.

So the Finns didn't hit the front of the column. They cut the road into pieces, then surrounded each piece. They called the trapped pockets motti, the word for a stack of firewood left to pick up later.
Finnish skiers in white snowsuits struck from the forest, hit the supply wagons and field kitchens, and vanished. The Soviet soldiers were stuck on the road, in the cold, with no way to move.
By late December, the 163rd was beaten. By January 7, the 44th was destroyed too. Together, the two battles cost the Soviets an estimated 22,000 to 27,000 men, plus more than 40 tanks.
Finland's most famous sniper was a farmer named Simo Häyhä. He was a prize-winning shot who hardly said a word. Soviet soldiers called him the White Death.
He's credited with more than 500 kills. Sniper counts are hard to prove, so treat that number as a legend with a military record behind it.
Finland had a joke for everything. Moscow's foreign minister, Molotov, claimed Soviet bombers were dropping food for hungry Finns. The Finns called the bombs Molotov's bread baskets.
Those bread baskets were real bombs. Each one was a big metal case that opened in the air and scattered small fire bombs over a city. Nobody was getting lunch.
So when Finns filled bottles with gasoline to throw at Soviet tanks, they named them Molotov cocktails. A drink to go with the bread.
Stalin wasn't laughing. In January, he doubled the force on the Finnish front, and put Marshal Timoshenko in charge of a new plan.
The new plan was simple and brutal. Infantry practiced working with tanks. Engineers practiced clearing the boulder traps. And then came the guns.

On February 1, Soviet artillery and bombers began pounding the Isthmus. For ten days the shells kept coming. By one estimate, more than 300,000 shells fell in a single day. The Finnish defenders lost about 3,000 men to the bombardment alone.
The Finns were worn out. They had few fresh troops and not much ammunition. On February 11, the Soviets attacked near Summa.
Soviet tanks and infantry broke through right next to Summa, at a place called Lähde. By February 15, Mannerheim ordered the Finns to give up the main line and fall back.
Soviet troops also crossed the frozen bay toward Viipuri, to get behind the Finns. Now the fight was for Viipuri, and Finland was running out of time.

Finland had asked the world for help. Weapons arrived from countries like Britain, France, Sweden, and the United States. But a British and French force never got through. Norway and Sweden wouldn't let it cross.
By early March, the Finnish army was close to collapse. The men were exhausted, and the artillery was running low on ammunition. Peace talks were the only road left.
On March 12, in Moscow, Finland signed a peace treaty. The fighting stopped at 11 AM, Helsinki time, on March 13. The war had lasted 105 days.
Finland gave up the whole Karelian Isthmus, including Viipuri, the Ladoga shore, and a slice near Salla. It also leased Hanko to the Soviets for 30 years.
That was about 11 percent of Finland's land. It was more than Stalin first asked for. But Helsinki still belonged to Finland, and so did its government.
Finland lost about 26,000 people, dead or missing. For the Soviet Union, estimates run from roughly 127,000 to more than 167,000, and nobody agrees on the real number.

beats.say: More than 400,000 Finns left the lost land. Nearly everyone chose to leave rather than live under Soviet rule, and they had to start over somewhere new.

The Red Army looked weak. Stalin's purges had wiped out many of its best officers, and its troops weren't ready for the cold. Many historians think this helped convince Hitler that invading the USSR would be easy.

Finland's neighbors across the Baltic weren't so lucky. Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania were soon swallowed up by the Soviet Union. Finland was not. The two countries would fight again in 1941, but that's another story.
So who actually won? The Soviets got the land. Finland kept its country. Which one counts as a win? Tell me in the comments.
